clue.text: Barrier isn't as much trouble feature of random choice

indicators.note: the words before are put to much trouble, that is, stirred up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a barrier causes as much bother as a random draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much trouble' tells you to rearrange BARRIER, ISNT and AS together; the 13 letters make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbitrariness is the quality of being decided by chance or whim, the hallmark of a random pick.

clue.text: Inept cook raged with heartfelt fury

indicators.note: the words are thrown into a fury, a wild state, so their letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bad cook loses their temper in a deeply felt rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fury' rearranges RAGED and HEARTFELT. Legend says this English king of Wessex, sheltering in a peasant's hut, let the cakes he was minding burn.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth-century king is famous from the legend of burning the cakes, so he is history's best-known careless cook.

clue.text: Dull combination using bishop and king

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.surface: A chess combination involving bishop and king that turns out dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Blear describes eyes or sight that are dim and blurred, so lacking brightness.

clue.text: Able to clarify views, or shut up as required

explanation.surface: Something that sharpens what you see, or folds away when told.
explanation.definitionFit: A telescope magnifies distant scenes, and its sections slide into one another, so the word covers both magnifying and collapsing in stages.

clue.text: Isn't part of wood overlapping racecourse?

indicators.note: the two words share a letter where they meet, so one copy of the shared letter goes

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't
a tree is one of the many that make up a wood

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a bit of woodland stretches over a course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlapping' means AINT and TREE share their T. AINTREE, near Liverpool, is where the Grand National steeplechase is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree is a famous English horse-racing course, home of the Grand National.

clue.text: Whereby Poles remain cool-headed?

parts.note: read 'Poles' as the Earth's north and south poles and 'cool-headed' as literally capped with something frozen

explanation.surface: Asks how people from Poland manage to keep calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like the people of Poland; it is the geographic poles, whose heads are covered with ice.
explanation.definitionFit: The frozen sheets covering the polar regions literally keep the tops of the globe cold.

clue.text: Jane's circuit

explanation.surface: A note on whose round or route belongs to a woman named Jane.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane is the heroine of Charlotte Brontë's novel, and an eyre was the circuit travelled by medieval itinerant judges.

clue.text: Supporting by temporarily moving? Doesn't sound like it

explanation.surface: A question of whether backing someone is the same as transferring them for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't sound like it' points out that the two senses are spelt alike but stressed differently: SEC-onding for backing, se-COND-ing for a temporary posting.
explanation.definitionFit: Backing a motion is seconding it, while an employee lent to another department for a time is said to be seconded.

clue.text: Convert Tories do acclaim if one left? Unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement of these words signals that their letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one, which must be left out of the mix

explanation.surface: Doubts whether Conservatives would cheer a defector if somebody quit.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TORIESDOACCLAIM, remove one I ('if one left'), and 'Unlikely' rearranges the rest. The British Social Democratic Party was founded in 1981 largely by converts from Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the new centre party of the early 1980s were typically defectors from other parties, so a party convert.

clue.text: Mercenary general's back in the country

indicators.note: the turned name sits inside the name of the country

parts.note: France is the country

indicators.note: the general's name is read backwards

parts.note: Lee was the Confederate general of the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A soldier for hire whose general has returned home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LEE into EEL, and 'in' places it inside FRANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A free lance was originally a knight who sold his services to any lord, the same as a hired soldier.

clue.text: Churchman cut page, right?

indicators.note: the churchman's title is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a rector is a parish priest

explanation.surface: A clergyman tore out a page and asks if that was right.
explanation.definitionFit: Recto is the right-hand page of an open book, the front of a leaf.

clue.text: "Cornish" heads include fifty nobles

indicators.note: the first piece contains the second within it

parts.note: the heads of corn are its ears, with the quotes flagging the play on Cornwall
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: The leaders of Cornwall count fifty aristocrats among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cornish' is not Cornwall but 'of corn': the heads of cereal plants are ears.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking above a viscount, so earls are titled aristocrats.

clue.text: Like Belloc's colourful sounding books?

indicators.note: the colour word is heard as a different word spelt another way

parts.note: red is a colour

explanation.surface: Asks what Hilaire Belloc's books were, in the manner of a vivid colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's mock epitaph runs 'His sins were scarlet, but his books were read', a pun on the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Books that people have gone through are perused, the boast of Belloc's couplet.

clue.text: Opponent's endless caper

indicators.note: the synonym for caper loses its final letter

parts.note: an antic is a playful caper or prank

explanation.surface: A rival is described as one never-ending prank.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is against a proposal is an opposer, used as a noun.

clue.text: Characters unaffected by reverse

parts.note: 'characters' are letters rather than people, and the reverse is reading them backwards

explanation.surface: People whose spirits are not dented by a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests resilient people and 'reverse' a setback; read them as letters that say the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase such as 'level' that reads the same in either direction keeps its letters intact when turned round.

clue.text: Highest part, of course, is excellent

parts.note: the top is the highest point
a golf course is divided into holes

explanation.surface: The top section of something is naturally first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally'; it is a golf course, made up of holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-hole is dated British slang for first-rate or splendid.

clue.text: Tuppence short in change within art business

indicators.note: the mixed letters go inside the two letters

parts.note: tuppence is two pence, two Ps

indicators.note: the words short in are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A gallery that is two pennies short when giving change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges SHORT IN into RINTSHO, and 'within' puts that between P and P. Tuppence is British for two pennies; P is the abbreviation for a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop selling printed pictures and engravings is a trade in art.

clue.text: Story, some say, about an affectionate pet

indicators.note: the story word goes round the two letters

parts.note: a spiel is a glib story or patter

explanation.surface: A tale people tell concerning a loving animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaniels are gun dogs famed for their devoted, loving nature as family dogs.

clue.text: In wood it is the best policy

indicators.note: the phrase it is goes inside the tree

parts.note: elm is a wood
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woodland saying, echoing 'honesty is the best policy'.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the proverb 'honesty is the best policy'; here the definition means a policy favouring the best people.
explanation.definitionFit: Elitism is the belief that power should go to a select, superior few.

clue.text: Used by bookmakers outside country

explanation.surface: Bookies standing outside in some land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bookmakers' suggests betting shops; it means bookbinders, who use this goatskin leather on the outside of books.
explanation.definitionFit: Morocco is a fine goatskin leather for binding books, and also the North African kingdom.

clue.text: Found on beach, it makes one run round Southend

indicators.note: the cricket score goes around the letter

parts.note: a single is one run in cricket
the end of the word south is its last letter

explanation.surface: A seaside find leads someone to run around Southend-on-Sea, an Essex resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southend' looks like the Essex resort; it is the end of 'south', H. In cricket a single is one run.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is the mass of small rounded pebbles lining many British coasts.

clue.text: White through and through but they can't stand the heat

definitions.text: White through and through but they can't stand the heat

parts.words: White through and through but they can't stand the heat
parts.note: figures made wholly of something white that melt away in warmth

explanation.surface: Sounds like a comment about thoroughly pale people who wilt in hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can't stand the heat' sounds like a figure of speech, but it is literal: these figures melt.
explanation.definitionFit: Figures built of packed snow are entirely white and melt when it gets warm.

clue.text: Top performer's turn — incredible!

indicators.note: the performer's word turns round, read backwards

parts.note: a star is a leading performer

explanation.surface: A headline act's routine described as amazing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' looks like a stage act; it is the signal to read STAR backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats is an exclamation of annoyance or disbelief, as in 'nonsense!'.

clue.text: Travel on a river in an old ship

indicators.note: in a down-style reading the travelling word comes after the others

parts.note: to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Journeying along a river aboard an ancient vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the legendary ship of Jason and the Argonauts.

clue.text: Sing this in prison

parts.note: the word 'Sing' followed by the repeat mark gives the name of a famous American jail

explanation.surface: Advice to burst into song while locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeat sign after 'Sing' makes 'Sing Sing', the New York state prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The repeat mark means 'the same again', so 'Sing' plus it reads as the jail's doubled name.

clue.text: Book champion has? Right

explanation.surface: A question about whether the winner holds a book, and a reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A publisher counts each book as one of its works, a champion holds the crown of the sport, and legal entitlement to property is ownership.

clue.text: No — even if odd, letters give news

indicators.note: the letters are put into an odd, unusual order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A denial that some letters bring tidings, odd or not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' looks like part of 'even if odd'; it rearranges NO and IF.
explanation.definitionFit: Info is short for information, the facts or tidings someone passes on.

clue.text: Wooden pail, so to speak

explanation.surface: A wooden bucket, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pail, so to speak' is 'pale' said the same way; ashen also means made of ash wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen describes something made from ash timber, and it means grey-faced or wan, which sounds like a bucket.

clue.text: Scarf assembled from 10 parts

indicators.note: the parts are put together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the answer to 10 across, a right-hand page

explanation.surface: A muffler made up from ten pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' is a cross-reference to 10 across; 'assembled' puts its letters with FROM in a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A comforter is an old word for a long woollen muffler worn round the neck.

clue.text: We, for example, stick firmly to statement

parts.note: we is a personal pronoun
to cement is to bond things fast

explanation.surface: Our group, say, holding firmly to an announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: A pronouncement is a formal declaration or announcement.
